headline: School bluefin on the Mud Hole lumps as mahi start showing on the pot lines
subhead: Warm blue water is pushing onto the ridge structure and the tuna bite is finally worth the run — but you still have to find the right lump.
body_markdown:
The bait told the story this week. Sandeels and small bunker are pinned tight against the drop-offs on the Mud Hole lumps where the cleaner blue water is holding underneath a warm lens — and the school bluefin found them. That's a pattern I've seen a dozen Julys now: wind-driven surface warming doesn't kill the bite, it just pushes it down and tightens it up onto structure. A few days of sloppy afternoon sea breeze pushed a layer of warm, slightly dirty green water over the inshore lumps, and for a while it looked like it might shove the tuna off the structure entirely. It didn't.

This week the moon's swinging toward first quarter, which means the tide swings are moderating — not the big springs we had around the full moon, but enough push to keep bait moving off the ridges on the ebb. Wind looks like it'll lay down some mornings before the sea breeze fills in again, which is exactly the window I want. If that pattern holds, the early morning troll before 10 a.m. on the lumps should stay the most consistent play. If the breeze fires early and stays hard out of the southwest, I'd shift plans to jigging structure in closer, where the sea state doesn't matter as much.

The bluefin have been showing on the classic Mud Hole lumps — the 60 to 90 foot rises inside the Hole where the bottom breaks up sharp. Small spreads of green machines and cedar plugs, nothing fancy, pulled at 5.5 to 6 knots have been doing the damage on schoolies in the 20 to 40 pound class. When the birds are working — and they have been most mornings — I've had better luck dropping the troll gear and jigging Shimano Butterfly jigs, the 100 to 150 gram in dark green/purple, straight down through the bait ball. That's put fish in the box on days the troll went quiet by 9. Klondike has been more hit or miss — a couple boats connected on the eastern edge where it drops toward the deeper water, but the bite there has been thinner and shorter-lived than the Mud Hole. I wouldn't make Klondike your only stop right now; treat it as a secondary check on the way out or back.

Mahi are just starting to show, which tracks with what I expect this time of year — the real stacking on the pot buoys and high flyers usually doesn't peak until August, but the first scouts are already showing up on the warm-water lines pushing along Barnegat Ridge and the outer edge off Manasquan. If you find floating debris or a lobster pot line holding bait underneath, slow down and pitch a small white bucktail or a chunk of butterfish on a spinning rod before you leave it. Most of what's come over the rail so far has been schoolies in the 3 to 6 pound range, nothing to write home about yet, but the pattern is building the right way — warmer water, more current-driven debris lines, more small mahi sightings each week. By early August I'd expect that bite to turn from a curiosity into a real target.

Black sea bass remain the most dependable meat in the box right now, and the jumbos have been sitting exactly where they always sit in mid-July — deep on the wreck structure, not the open reef sand. Triple Wrecks has been the standout, sea bass to 4 and 5 pounds coming off the high structure in 110 to 140 feet on Gulp Grub/squid combos fished on a two-hook bottom rig with 6 to 8 ounces of lead depending on the drift. Sea Girt Reef and Axel Carlson have also been productive but the average size skews smaller — good numbers of keepers in the 14 to 16 inch range, with the occasional jumbo mixed in on the deeper pieces. If you're after quality over quantity, the wreck iron beats the open reef right now — the bigger fish are holding tight to vertical structure, not spread out on the sand.

Bonito have started trickling onto the shallower reef structure — Shrewsbury Rocks and the inshore end of Sea Girt Reef have both produced a few on small metal jigs and Deadly Dick lures worked fast through bait showers. It's early and scattered, more a sign of things to come than a real target yet, but worth a few casts if you're already anchored up on sea bass and see fish snapping on top.

One honest note — blackfish season is closed right now in state waters, so don't waste a trip planning around tog. That fishery comes back in the fall and it's worth the wait; the wrecks holding jumbo sea bass now are the same pieces that'll load up with big tog once the water cools and the season reopens.

Looking ahead, if the morning wind lays down like the forecast suggests, I'd be on the Mud Hole lumps at first light chasing bluefin under the birds, then working the pot lines on the way in checking for mahi. If the breeze comes up early, Plan B is simple — anchor on Triple Wrecks or Sea Girt Reef and fill the cooler with sea bass while the tuna bite sorts itself out. Either way there's enough happening on the structure right now to make the run worth it.
